habitat: Reedbeds and sedges, solitary or scattered. It is diurnal, hard to flush, and sky-points to avoid detection.
summary: A tiny bittern. The male has bold black-edged wings. The female has a buffy neck and a black cap. The immature is paler and less rufous below than a young Dwarf Bittern, with olive rather than orange-yellow legs, and has tawny folded wings rather than the dark wings of a young Green-backed Heron. In flight the black and buff wings are the mark. Newman calls it an uncommon resident and visitor, and nomadic.

similar.note: Dwarf Bittern is slate-grey above with heavily streaked underparts and orange-yellow legs. A young Little Bittern is paler and less rufous below, with olive legs.
A young Green-backed Heron has dark folded wings. A young Little Bittern has tawny folded wings.

population.notes: Kemp et al. 2001 order-of-magnitude threshold 2^3=8 mature individuals (non-breeding visitor); paper interval half–double → 4–16.

sources.title: Kemp A.C., Herholdt J.J., Whyte I. & Harrison J. (2001). Birds of the two largest national parks in South Africa: a method to generate estimates of population size for all species and assess their conservation ecology. S. Afr. J. Sci. 97: 393–403.

calls.description: Newman does not describe the voice. The texts do not separate the sexes. The catalogue cut is not labelled by sex. Grade A from France, under the older genus Ixobrychus. No Botaurus minutus recording was in the catalogue.

research.note: Status is resident and all twelve months are listed. Newman calls it both an uncommon resident and a visitor, and nomadic, without a month of absence. Chick down is not described. The call is grade A from France. The photograph matches the female description and is tagged female.
